page_hint: Ch 20, aggregate-rps note (end of chapter, after Fig 20.1)
quoted_clause: the 21/22-host planning sizing, which delivers ≈ 41.5 rps ≈ 1.04× peak
observed: The numbers 41.5 and 1.04 match the 21-host analytical capacity (21 × 17/8.6 = 41.52; 41.52/40 = 1.038 ≈ 1.04) but not the 22-host ρ-derated capacity (22 × 17/8.6 × 0.95 = 41.31; 41.31/40 = 1.033 ≈ 1.03). The phrase '21/22-host' is ambiguous about which sizing the figures refer to.
root_cause: Ambiguous antecedent for '21/22-host planning sizing' combined with rounding that happens to match one reading better than the other.
correction: Disambiguate: e.g. 'the 21-host ideal sizing delivers ≈41.5 rps ≈1.04× peak (the 22-host ρ-derated sizing delivers ≈41.3 rps ≈1.03× peak)'.
acceptance_test: Recompute both 21-host and 22-host capacities; confirm the printed numbers match the intended host count.

page_hint: Ch 20 §1 (Concept) vs §3 (Worked Example, fleet aggregate formula)
quoted_clause: aggregate system throughput is not merely the sum of individual host throughputs; it is modulated by scheduling overhead, network contention, and the cost of moving data between hosts and storage
observed: §1 states that aggregate throughput is not merely N × Q, but §3 then presents Λ_fleet = N × Q as the fleet formula without explicitly stating that ρ = 0.95 (or any other derate) is the mechanism that accounts for the scheduling/network overheads §1 mentions. The reader must infer the connection.
evidence: §1: 'not merely the sum… modulated by scheduling overhead, network contention…'. §3: 'Λ_fleet = N × Q' labelled 'illustrative form'. The ρ = 0.95 derate appears later in the same paragraph but is not explicitly tied back to the §1 overheads.
root_cause: The overhead narrative in §1 and the derate in §3 are not explicitly linked.
correction: Add one sentence at the Λ_fleet = N × Q formula: e.g. 'The ρ ≈ 0.95 derate below is the first-order correction for the scheduling and network overheads §1 describes; Λ_fleet = N × Q is the pre-derate ideal.'
acceptance_test: Read §1 → §3 transition; confirm the reader can identify which term in §3 accounts for the §1 overheads.

quoted_clause: A suboptimal batch size on one host can increase dispatch frequency for the entire fleet.
observed: The causal mechanism is unclear. A suboptimal batch size on one host makes that host process requests slower; it is not obvious why this would increase the *dispatch frequency* (rate of scheduler decisions) for the entire fleet rather than, say, shifting load to other hosts or increasing queue depth on the slow host.
evidence: No mechanism is given. The preceding sentence ('ignores the scheduling overhead that becomes dominant when the fleet is viewed as a unit') is about a different failure mode (per-host optimisation ignoring fleet-level overhead).
root_cause: Vague causal claim in a Common Mistakes bullet.
correction: Either specify the mechanism (e.g. 'a slow host forces the scheduler to re-balance more frequently, increasing dispatch decisions per unit time') or replace with a clearer example (e.g. 'a suboptimal batch size on one host creates a straggler that inflates fleet p99 even when aggregate throughput is ample').
acceptance_test: Read the bullet; confirm the reader can state the causal chain from 'suboptimal batch size on one host' to 'increased dispatch frequency for the entire fleet'.

page_hint: Ch 20 §6, subsection 'The useful completion is an accepted clip'
quoted_clause: The same accepted-completion goodput accounting applies to any fixed-output-contract workload; a video-generation fleet is the clearest parallel beyond RAG.
observed: This subsection (~4 paragraphs) introduces an entirely new workload class (video generation) with its own vocabulary (clips, frames, denoising, reconstruction, sequence-parallel groups, encoder loading) that appears nowhere else in the chapter or, based on this chunk, elsewhere in the book. It sits inside §6 (Architecture Consequence) after the three numbered points, breaking the flow of the RAG-fleet architecture narrative. The transferable insight — goodput for fixed-output-contract workloads — is valuable, but the video-specific detail (frame counts, clip-seconds/s denominators, heterogeneous preview/denoising/reconstruction pools) is breadth rather than architectural leverage for this chapter.
evidence: The subsection is ~4 paragraphs, introduces ≥8 new domain-specific terms, and none of the subsequent sections (§7 What We Still Don't Know, §8 Mini-Case) reference video generation again. The chapter's Architect's Question, Mental Model, Worked Example, Measurement, and Mini-Case are all RAG Q&A.
root_cause: A transfer-of-reasoning example was placed inline rather than as a brief pointer or a dedicated workload-diversity section.
correction: Either (a) compress to 1–2 sentences that state the transferable principle ('for fixed-output-contract workloads, count accepted completions, not raw output tokens — the same goodput logic applies to video clips, batch jobs, or any deadline-bounded output') and drop the video-specific detail, or (b) move the full subsection to a chapter on workload diversity / goodput where it can be developed properly with its own figure and mini-case.
acceptance_test: Confirm the chapter's Architect's Question is fully answered without the video subsection; confirm the transferable goodput principle is still stated.

quoted_clause: prefill FLOPs per request (full-square attention, conservative) | ~1.5099 PFLOP | 1.288 + 4 ×80 ×9,200² ×8,192 = 1.288 + 0.2219 (+17.23%)
observed: The table’s expression omits the multiplication by the number of layers in the written form: the attention term is 4·n_layers·L²·d, i.e. 4×80×9,200²×8,192. The printed expression “4 ×80 ×9,200² ×8,192” is arithmetically correct if read as 4×80×9,200²×8,192, but the surrounding text and Note 22.1-1 use 4·n_layers·L²·d. The table’s “1.288 + 0.2219” is correct; the issue is only that the displayed expression can be misread as 4×80×9,200²×8,192 without the layer factor being visually separated.
evidence: Note 22.1-1: “Full-square: the quadratic attention term 4·n_layers·L²·d equals the parameterized-linear term 2N·L at L* = N/(2·n_layers·d).” The table’s numeric result 0.2219 PFLOP is consistent with 4×80×9,200²×8,192. This is a presentation/legibility issue, not a numerical error.
root_cause: The table’s inline expression is compressed and does not visually separate the layer count from the rest of the attention term.
correction: Rewrite the table entry as “1.288 + 4·80·(9,200)²·8,192 = 1.288 + 0.2219 (+17.23%)” or add a parenthetical “(4·n_layers·L²·d with n_layers=80, d=8,192)”.
acceptance_test: Check that a reader can reproduce 0.2219 PFLOP from the printed expression without consulting Note 22.1-1, and that the expression explicitly identifies n_layers=80 and d=8,192.

quoted_clause: Before passing this workload to Chapter 7 (Memory), where the KV and residency arithmetic is built, the architect locks in one more number
observed: The phrasing implies Chapter 7 comes after Chapter 22 in reading order, which is false. The reader is at Ch 22 having already read Ch 7 and used its KV arithmetic extensively (Table 22-1 already includes KV cache memory per request). The mini-case appears to replay the early-book workflow from scratch, as if the reader has not yet reached Ch 7.
evidence: Chapter 7 precedes Chapter 22 in the book's structure. Table 22-1 in this same chapter already lists 'KV cache memory per request ~24.1 GB' — derived using Ch 7's arithmetic. The mini-case then says 'before passing to Ch 7 where the KV arithmetic is built,' contradicting the reader's actual position.
root_cause: The mini-case narrates the architect's workflow as if it maps linearly to the book's chapter order, but the mini-case is at Ch 22 while the workflow step it describes corresponds to Ch 7.
correction: Reframe to acknowledge the reader's position: 'In the architect's workflow, the next step after locking token counts is memory sizing (the arithmetic the book built in Ch 7). Before that step, the architect records the tokens-per-request split.' Or simply remove the Ch 7 forward-reference and state the workflow step directly.
acceptance_test: Verify the mini-case does not imply Ch 7 follows Ch 22 in reading order, and that the workflow narrative is consistent with the reader's actual position in the book.

page_hint: Ch 22 Table 22-1, row 'decode required BW rate'
quoted_clause: decode required BW rate | ~5.6 TB/s | ~140 GB / 25 ms TPOT (= traffic / decode interval)
observed: The table presents ~5.6 TB/s as 'the decode required BW rate' without noting this is only the weight-read component. Total decode bandwidth demand also includes KV-cache reads at each decode step, which at high concurrency can substantially exceed the weight-read component. A reader consulting Table 22-1 as a reference might interpret 5.6 TB/s as the total decode bandwidth requirement.
evidence: At 17.5 concurrent requests on one host (the FP16 KV residency ceiling), KV read per GPU per step = 17.5 × 24.9/8 = 54.5 GB; over 25 ms = 2.18 TB/s. Weight read per GPU = 0.70 TB/s. Total ≈ 2.88 TB/s out of 3.35 TB/s HBM peak — KV reads are ~3× the weight reads. The table's 5.6 TB/s (aggregate weight-read only) captures ~20% of the total decode bandwidth demand at this operating point.
root_cause: The table row label 'decode required BW rate' is broader than the derivation, which computes only the weight-read component (140 GB / 25 ms).
correction: Rename the row to 'decode weight-read BW rate' or add a scope note: 'weight-read component only; KV-cache read bandwidth is additional and scales with concurrency (Ch 6/8).' Alternatively, add a separate row for total decode bandwidth at the canonical operating point.
acceptance_test: Verify the table row label or note explicitly scopes the 5.6 TB/s figure to the weight-read component and directs the reader to where total decode bandwidth (weight + KV) is discussed.

page_hint: Ch 22 §7 What We Still Don't Know
quoted_clause: Prefill FLOP cost under continuous batching — Chapter 2 §7; the 2 × params × tokens approximation ignores activation reuse across batched requests. (a hypothesis awaiting verification)
observed: Three of four items use the parenthetical label '(a hypothesis awaiting verification)' while the fourth uses bracket tags '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]'. Additionally, some claims labeled as hypotheses are stated as facts: 'the 2 × params × tokens approximation ignores activation reuse' is a factual property of the formula, not a hypothesis. The hypothesis would be about the magnitude of the effect, not the existence of the omission.
evidence: Item 1: '(a hypothesis awaiting verification)' — appropriate (real kernels may sustain less than peak). Item 2: '(a hypothesis awaiting verification)' — the claim that the formula 'ignores' something is factual; the hypothesis is about effect size. Item 3: '(a hypothesis awaiting verification)' — 'quantization shifts both bottlenecks' is stated as fact. Item 4: '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]' — different label vocabulary entirely.
root_cause: Inconsistent evidence-label vocabulary within a single section, and misapplication of 'hypothesis' to factual claims about formula properties.
correction: Unify the label vocabulary across all four items. For item 2, reframe: 'the magnitude of activation-reuse savings under continuous batching is workload-dependent (to be verified).' For item 3, similarly separate the factual claim from the open question. Use one label format consistently.
acceptance_test: All four items in Ch 22 §7 use the same evidence-label format, and each label correctly characterizes the epistemic status of the claim (hypothesis vs. fact vs. derived).

quoted_clause: Ch 22: '(a hypothesis awaiting verification)' / Ch 23: '(to be verified)' and '(a hypothesis)' / Ch 24: table with 'Planned investigation' / Ch 25: numbered list, no labels
observed: The four 'What We Still Don't Know' sections in this chunk use four different formats and at least three different evidence-label vocabularies: parenthetical labels (Ch 22), mixed parenthetical labels (Ch 23), table format (Ch 24), and unlabeled numbered list (Ch 25). The book's evidence-label vocabulary (per house conventions: [CANONICAL] [DERIVED] [ILLUSTRATIVE] [ASSUMPTION] [1P] [HYPOTHESIS]) is not consistently applied.
evidence: Ch 22 uses '(a hypothesis awaiting verification)' and '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]'. Ch 23 uses '(to be verified)' and '(a hypothesis)'. Ch 24 uses a table with no evidence labels on individual items. Ch 25 uses a numbered list with no evidence labels.
root_cause: Each chapter's 'What We Still Don't Know' section was written independently without a shared format or label specification.
correction: Define one format and label vocabulary for 'What We Still Don't Know' sections and apply it consistently across all chapters. At minimum, each item should carry one of the house-convention labels ([HYPOTHESIS], [ASSUMPTION], etc.) and use a consistent structural format.
acceptance_test: All 'What We Still Don't Know' sections use the same structural format and evidence-label vocabulary.

page_hint: Ch 22 Fig 22.1 figure note (italicized paragraph after Note 22.1-1)
quoted_clause: at 9.2K the quadratic attention term is ~17% of the parameterized-linear 2NL term (so it is still subordinate), at 128K it is ~2.4× the linear term (attention relative to linear), and total prefill FLOPs at 128K are ~3.4× the 2NL baseline
observed: The ratios ~17% (at 9.2K), ~2.4× (at 128K), and ~3.4× (total at 128K) are all full-square counting figures but the text does not specify the counting convention for these particular ratios. Under causal-triangle counting, the corresponding values would be ~8.6%, ~1.2×, and ~2.2×. The Note 22.1-1 above explicitly distinguishes the two conventions for the crossover points but the figure note's ratios do not carry this qualification.
evidence: Full-square at 9.2K: 0.2219/1.288 = 17.2%. Causal-triangle at 9.2K: 0.1109/1.288 = 8.6%. Full-square at 128K: 4×80×128000×8192/(2×70e9) = 2.40×. Causal-triangle at 128K: 1.20×. Total full-square at 128K: 1+2.4 = 3.4×. Total causal-triangle at 128K: 1+1.2 = 2.2×.
root_cause: The figure note presents ratios without specifying which FLOP-counting convention they use, even though Note 22.1-1 immediately above makes this distinction for the crossover points.
correction: Add '(full-square counting)' to the ratio statements, or provide both conventions: '~17% (full-square) / ~8.6% (causal-triangle) at 9.2K.'
acceptance_test: Every ratio in the figure note specifies its FLOP-counting convention, consistent with Note 22.1-1's treatment of the crossover points.

quoted_clause: the canonical ~2,000 user, ~10 rps / ~40 rps peak, RAG Q&A, 70B dense FP16 scenario
observed: '~2,000 user' should be '~2,000 users' (if read as a list item) or '~2,000-user' (if read as a compound adjective). As written, 'user' is singular after a plural number without hyphenation.
evidence: Standard English: '2,000 users' (plural noun) or '2,000-user scenario' (hyphenated compound adjective).
root_cause: Typo or missing plural/hyphen.
correction: Change to '~2,000-user' (hyphenated compound modifier) or '~2,000 users'.
acceptance_test: Grammar check passes for the phrase.

quoted_clause: a ~140 GB/token weight-read requiring ~5.6 TB/s sustained over the ~25 ms decode interval — an aggregate single-device figure
observed: 'Aggregate single-device figure' is oxymoronic: 'aggregate' implies whole-model/multi-device scope while 'single-device' implies one device. The intent is 'the whole-model figure before sharding, as if computed for a single device doing everything.' The same scoping point is made more clearly in the figure note: 'the aggregate (whole-model) linear-only deadline demand.'
evidence: 5.6 TB/s = 140 GB (whole model) / 25 ms. This is the whole-model figure. With 8-GPU tensor parallelism, each GPU streams 0.70 TB/s. 'Aggregate' and 'single-device' pull in opposite directions.
root_cause: Terminology imprecision in describing the scope of the bandwidth figure.
correction: Replace with 'a whole-model figure (before tensor-parallel sharding)' or 'the aggregate figure if one device read all weights,' consistent with the figure note's clearer phrasing.
acceptance_test: The scope descriptor unambiguously communicates that 5.6 TB/s is the whole-model figure before sharding.

quoted_clause: a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s, with a 200-rps burst buffer, quality-gated on real resolved tickets — and a two-week pilot on 5% of tickets to confirm the referral quality before full rollout.
observed: The mini-case states a 200-rps burst alongside a single on-prem GPU and a 7B-class model. If “200-rps burst buffer” means the GPU must serve 200 requests/s, the prefill demand alone is 200×500=100,000 input tokens/s. For a 7B model, prefill FLOPs are 2×7×10⁹×500=7×10¹² FLOP/request, so 200 rps requires 1.4×10¹⁵ FLOP/s=1.4 PFLOPS, above one H100’s dense FP16 peak (~0.989 PFLOPS) and far above a realistic 30–40% MFU. The phrase “burst buffer” may mean a queue that absorbs bursts rather than a served rate, but the sentence does not distinguish buffered arrivals from served throughput.
evidence: The same chapter’s canonical arithmetic uses 2×params×tokens for prefill. At 500 tokens and 7B parameters, one request is ~7 TFLOP; 200 rps is ~1.4 PFLOPS. One H100 dense FP16 peak is ~0.989 PFLOPS (Ch 8 canonical). The text does not state the output length, batching, or whether the 200-rps burst is queued rather than served.
root_cause: The mini-case uses “200-rps burst buffer” without defining whether 200 rps is an arrival rate absorbed by a queue or a served rate on the single GPU. The surrounding arithmetic is not shown, so the feasibility of the single-GPU recommendation is ambiguous.
correction: Clarify that the 200-rps burst is an arrival/buffer requirement, not a sustained served rate on one GPU; state the queueing/SLO assumption and the expected drain time, or revise the hardware recommendation if 200 rps is intended as a served rate.
acceptance_test: Recompute the single-GPU prefill capacity for 500-token, 7B requests at the stated MFU; show that the 200-rps burst is either buffered (with a stated queue and drain-time assumption) or infeasible on one GPU, and make the text state which interpretation is intended.

quoted_clause: → Bound 1: ~2,000 users, ~10 rps average, ~40 rps peak.
observed: The customer states ~40 rps peak ('maybe 40 a second') but never states an average rate. The ~10 rps average appears in Bound 1 without derivation from the dialogue. The architect says 'realistically a fraction of that firing requests' but never quantifies the fraction or derives the average.
evidence: Dialogue trace: Architect asks about peak → customer says 40 → Bound 1 includes both 10 rps average and 40 rps peak. The 10 rps figure matches the canonical scenario but its derivation from the conversation is absent. Possible derivation: 100 concurrent × 1 request per ~10 s = 10 rps, but this is not shown.
root_cause: The worked example is constructed to match the canonical scenario, and the average rate was inserted to complete the bound without showing how the architect would extract or derive it from the conversation.
correction: Add a derivation step in the dialogue: Architect: 'And on an average day, roughly how many questions per second?' Lead: 'Maybe 10 a second, busier in the morning.' → Bound 1: ~10 rps average. Or show the architect deriving it: 'If ~100 are active and each asks every ~10 seconds, that's ~10 rps average — does that sound right?'
acceptance_test: Every number in Bound 1 traces to either a customer statement or an explicit architect derivation within the dialogue.

quoted_clause: → Bound 5: operational constraint forces the local/server tier (Ch13).
observed: The customer says 'keep it on-prem if at all possible' — a preference with an escape clause — plus 'It's internal and regulated' — a hard constraint. The architect's Bound 5 uses 'forces,' converting the preference into an absolute constraint without separating the hard constraint (regulated) from the soft one (if at all possible).
evidence: Customer's exact words: 'It's internal and regulated; keep it on-prem if at all possible.' The 'regulated' clause justifies a hard constraint; 'if at all possible' signals flexibility. Bound 5 collapses both into 'forces.'
root_cause: The dialogue presents a hard constraint and a preference in the same utterance, and the architect's bound treats them as one absolute constraint.
correction: Separate the constraints in the bound: 'Bound 5a: regulated data → on-prem required (hard). Bound 5b: on-prem preferred if possible (soft — cloud fallback acceptable if regulated-data controls are met).' Or have the architect probe: 'Is on-prem a hard requirement because of regulation, or a preference?'
acceptance_test: Bound 5 distinguishes hard constraints from preferences, and the dialogue shows the architect probing which is which.

quoted_clause: TTFT ≤ 2 s, ~25 ms/token
observed: The dialogue's Bound 3 includes 'p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms' but Table 23-1's SLO row omits it, showing only 'TTFT ≤ 2 s, ~25 ms/token'. The table is presented as a summary of the six bounds, so the omission makes the table an incomplete summary of Bound 3.
evidence: Dialogue Bound 3: 'TTFT ≤ 2 s (p95), ~25 ms/token thereafter (mean decode budget; p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms, Ch 4).' Table 23-1: 'TTFT ≤ 2 s, ~25 ms/token.'
root_cause: The table row was abbreviated without noting the omission.
correction: Add 'p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms' to the table row, or add a footnote: 'p95 TPOT ≤ 35 ms also applies (see dialogue).'
acceptance_test: Table 23-1 SLO row includes all latency components stated in Bound 3 of the dialogue.

quoted_clause: quality means "resolve the ticket, not just answer" (a capability the cheaper model screens out)
observed: Grammatically ambiguous: 'a capability the cheaper model screens out' can be read as (a) a capability that screens out the cheaper model [intended], or (b) a capability that the cheaper model screens out [filters something]. The intended meaning is (a) — the quality requirement eliminates cheaper models — but the phrasing supports reading (b).
evidence: Parse (a): '[resolve the ticket] is a capability [that] the cheaper model [is] screened out [by]' — the capability causes the cheaper model to be rejected. Parse (b): 'a capability [that] the cheaper model screens out' — the cheaper model filters this capability. Both parses are grammatically valid.
root_cause: Ambiguous relative clause attachment.
correction: Rewrite for clarity: '(a capability that eliminates the cheaper model)' or '(which rules out the cheaper model)'.
acceptance_test: The phrase has only one natural grammatical reading.

quoted_clause: After deduplication by normalized edit distance at a fixed threshold (we use normalized Levenshtein distance ≤ 0.25 as the equivalence criterion), the unique exposure surface is **PIES = 217** [ILLUSTRATIVE] — author-defined operational proxy; the 217 is not reproducible from the text alone, since the dedup threshold is a local choice, the greedy assignment is order-sensitive (generation order, representative selection, and tie-break are unspecified), and normalized edit distance captures textual, not semantic, similarity.
observed: The chapter correctly labels PIES as an order-sensitive, author-defined heuristic and says 217 is not reproducible from the text alone. But §8 then compares PIES values across cycles (217 → 143 → 138) and states “both values from the same order-sensitive dedup heuristic, compared under a fixed generation order.” The text does not state the fixed generation order, representative-selection rule, tie-break rule, or normalization denominator, so the cross-cycle comparison is not reproducible from the printed record. The caveat is present, but the mini-case’s quantitative trend is still presented as a measured improvement.
evidence: §3.1: “Without a canonical generation order, normalization denominator, representative-selection rule, stable sort, tie-break rule, and test fixture, the count is well-defined only within a single fixed run.” §8: “PIES has dropped from 217 to 143 … (both values from the same order-sensitive dedup heuristic, compared under a fixed generation order — §3.1).” The fixed order is asserted but not specified.
root_cause: The chapter acknowledges the reproducibility gap but then uses the PIES trend as a quantitative outcome without supplying the missing fixed-run parameters.
correction: Either provide the fixed generation order, normalization denominator, representative-selection rule, stable sort, tie-break rule, and test fixture in the text or an appendix, or downgrade the 217→143→138 trend to an explicitly non-reproducible illustrative sequence and avoid treating the drop as evidence of guardrail effectiveness.
acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 217, 143, and 138 from the printed rules and a stated probe corpus/order; if not, the text must not present the PIES drop as a measured or comparable result.

quoted_clause: A100 (and the 8×H100 host) natively supports BF16 and TF32 on its Tensor Cores. There is no "next GPU generation" required and no explicit-casting penalty; the premise that these formats wait for future hardware is itself the kind of error an ADR should catch.
observed: The ADR is about a 70B model on an 8×H100 host, but the rationale cites “A100 (and the 8×H100 host)” as if A100 and H100 are interchangeable evidence for native BF16/TF32 support. The canonical host is H100, not A100. The sentence is not numerically wrong, but it weakens the ADR’s evidence chain by mixing GPU generations in a decision record whose context is explicitly 8×H100.
evidence: ADR 0016 Context: “The fleet runs a 70-billion-parameter dense model for RAG Q&A serving on an 8×H100 host (640 GB).” The rationale then says “A100 (and the 8×H100 host) natively supports BF16 and TF32.” The H100 support is the relevant fact; the A100 reference is extraneous and could confuse readers about which hardware was validated.
root_cause: The ADR’s evidence sentence mixes A100 and H100 support without separating the canonical host from a prior-generation example.
correction: Rewrite to “H100 Tensor Cores natively support BF16 and TF32; A100 also supports them, but the canonical host here is 8×H100.” Or remove the A100 reference from the decision rationale.
acceptance_test: Check that every hardware-support claim in ADR 0016 names the canonical 8×H100 host explicitly and does not rely on A100 as a substitute for H100 evidence.

quoted_clause: plus ~30 GB activations at the peak for this worked example, giving ≈ 170 GB total derived footprint... Derived from the model parameter count and a typical activation overhead factor.
observed: The ~30 GB activation figure is presented as a derived quantity but its derivation is not shown. 'A typical activation overhead factor' is not defined — what is the factor? 30/140 = 21.4%? Where does this come from? For a section explicitly about derived quantities and evidence discipline, not showing the derivation of a key number is a gap.
evidence: The text says 'Derived from the model parameter count and a typical activation overhead factor' but does not state the factor, its source, or the calculation. 30 GB / 140 GB = 0.214, but this ratio is not stated or sourced.
root_cause: The activation figure is an illustrative estimate presented in a section that emphasizes derived quantities, but the derivation is elided.
correction: Either show the derivation explicitly (e.g., 'activation working set ≈ 2 × batch × seq_len × hidden × n_layers × bytes — for the canonical single-request prefill at 9.2K tokens this yields ~30 GB') or relabel it as [ASSUMPTION] rather than presenting it as derived.
acceptance_test: The ~30 GB figure either has a visible derivation with defined inputs, or is labeled as an assumption rather than a derived quantity.

quoted_clause: A100 (and the 8×H100 host) natively supports BF16 and TF32 on its Tensor Cores.
observed: The ADR is specifically about an 8×H100 deployment (stated in Context: 'serving on an 8×H100 host'). Mentioning A100 in the rationale is confusing — the reader wonders why a different GPU is relevant to this decision. The point (BF16 support is not new) could be made without naming A100, or the A100 reference could be explicitly framed as historical context.
evidence: ADR Context: 'The fleet runs a 70-billion-parameter dense model for RAG Q&A serving on an 8×H100 host (640 GB).' Rationale: 'A100 (and the 8×H100 host) natively supports BF16 and TF32.'
root_cause: The rationale addresses a hypothetical misconception ('these formats wait for future hardware') by citing A100 as evidence that BF16 has been supported for years, but the ADR's scope is H100.
correction: Either remove the A100 mention ('The 8×H100 host natively supports BF16 and TF32 on its Tensor Cores — no hardware upgrade is needed') or explicitly frame it: 'BF100 support dates back to the A100 generation; the H100 host certainly supports it natively.'
acceptance_test: The ADR rationale does not introduce hardware outside the deployment scope without explicit framing of why it is mentioned.

quoted_clause: RQO (Reasoned Quality Optimization): the discipline of improving an architecture decision's quality
observed: The acronym RQO is introduced and defined in this bullet, but it does not appear elsewhere in this chunk. If it was defined in an earlier chapter, this is a re-definition (acceptable); if not, it is a new acronym introduced late in the book for a concept that appears only here, which raises the question of whether the acronym earns its place.
evidence: RQO appears only in Ch 25 §6 within this chunk. No prior definition is visible. External chapters NOT VERIFIED.
root_cause: Either a late introduction of a previously defined term (fine) or a one-off acronym for a concept used only once (questionable value).
correction: If RQO is defined earlier, add a cross-reference. If it appears only here, consider whether the acronym adds value over simply describing the discipline in prose.
acceptance_test: RQO either has a prior definition with cross-reference, or is replaced by prose if it appears only once in the book.

quoted_clause: With tensor parallelism across the 8 H100s, a single host serves the model and can hold ~17.5 concurrent 9,500-token requests within the canonical ~436 GB KV budget from Chapter 15.
observed: The chapter reuses the canonical ~436 GB KV budget and ~17.5 concurrent 9,500-token requests, but the worked example in §8 explicitly declares a distinct short-prompt workload, not the canonical 9.2K-input case. The 17.5 figure is therefore a canonical-scenario value, not a property of the capstone's short-prompt workload.
evidence: §3 Pattern A states the canonical 9,500-token request count. §8 Step 1 says: 'The capstone declares a distinct short-prompt workload — it is not the canonical 9.2K-input/1.08-s-prefill case of Ch 4.' It then says the canonical C ≈ 17.5 and ~2.0 req/s ceiling are held as conservative planning caps. The text is careful about this in §8, but §3's Pattern A sentence reads as if the capstone host holds 17.5 concurrent 9,500-token requests.
